explanation.surface: A sports coach explains that exercise drills come down to number-crunching.
explanation.definitionFit: A session of physical training is a work-out, and to work out a sum is to calculate it.

parts.note: suggests great literary peaks, but means the windswept Yorkshire moorland farmhouse named in Emily Brontë's novel title

explanation.surface: A reference to the great summits of written art.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel is 'Wuthering Heights', so the word in front of 'Heights' is wanted; 'heights' looks like praise but is half the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in Emily Brontë's title describes the Heights, the farmhouse at the novel's centre.

clue.text: He reasons one should limit a catalogue

parts.note: to ration something is to limit how much is allowed
a catalogue is a list of items

explanation.surface: A thinker argues that any catalogue ought to be kept short.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who bases belief on reason rather than faith is a rationalist, a person who reasons.

clue.text: The way colonists also start to operate

explanation.surface: Settlers in a new land get a business going too.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonists open up new territory, making it accessible, and a shop or business that begins trading is said to open up.

parts.note: an ottoman is a footstool, but Ottoman also names the ... empire

explanation.surface: A fancy upholstered footstool in a drawing room.
explanation.walkthrough: The lower-case 'ottoman' suggests furniture; the sultan of the Ottoman Empire was known as the Grand Turk.
explanation.definitionFit: A subject of the Ottoman Empire was a native of Turkey, so an Ottoman is one of that nation.

explanation.surface: A note on what clothing suits horses that race over fences.
explanation.definitionFit: Woollen pullovers are jumpers in British English, and steeplechase horses leap fences, so they are jumpers too.

clue.text: Jazz occasion is not for today

definitions.text: Jazz occasion is not for today

parts.words: Jazz occasion is not for today
parts.note: recalls the White Queen's rule in Through the Looking-Glass, 'jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today', applied to an improvised jazz gathering

explanation.surface: Someone postpones a jazz gig to another day.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll's White Queen offers 'jam tomorrow and jam yesterday, but never jam today', so a session of jam is never for today.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal gathering where jazz musicians improvise together is known by this name.

clue.text: Mum at home has to remain as a supporter

parts.note: Ma is a familiar word for one's mother
to be in is to be at home
to stay is to remain

explanation.surface: A mother who stays at home supports the family.
explanation.definitionFit: A chief support or prop, originally the rope bracing a ship's mainmast, is a mainstay.

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from the opening of Browning's 'Love Among the Ruins'; the missing noun is the close of the day

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's 'Love Among the Ruins' opens 'Where the quiet-coloured end of evening smiles'.
explanation.definitionFit: The close or finish of evening is its end, the word Browning used.

clue.text: That's the stuff to give, a Russian!

explanation.surface: Someone hands over a gift to a man from Moscow, praising the goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' in the old sense means cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard-wearing twilled woollen cloth is serge, and the same word is the Russian man's name Sergei in its common English form.

clue.text: This little pig was the tenth

definitions.text: This little pig was the tenth

parts.words: This little pig was the tenth
parts.note: echoes the nursery rhyme 'This little piggy', but recalls the old church levy where every tenth piglet in a litter went to the parson

explanation.surface: A twist on the nursery rhyme counting off little piggies, now up to number ten.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme's 'little pig' is a red herring: under the old church levy a farmer handed over one pig in ten, the so-called tithe pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce or livestock paid to the church.

clue.text: The rest of the publishing world

explanation.surface: Someone sniffily dismisses everybody else in the book trade.
explanation.definitionFit: What is left over is the remainder, and publishers sell unsold stock cheaply as remainders.

parts.note: reads like a record-breaking trek over sand, but means the written account of the Israelites' journey through the wilderness

explanation.surface: A headline about someone crossing a desert in record time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' is a noun, a written account, not a record-breaking feat: the second book of the Bible records Moses leading Israel out of Egypt across the desert.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament book telling of the departure from Egypt and the wilderness wandering bears this title.

explanation.surface: A reader complains that a clergyman in a novel smells faintly of brimstone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shirley' is Charlotte Brontë's 1849 novel, whose rector is the Reverend Matthewson Helstone; the second sense reads the name as 'hell stone', i.e. brimstone, the sulphur of hell.
explanation.definitionFit: The parson in Brontë's novel is so named, and a hell-stone suggests the brimstone of the pit, hence a whiff of sulphur.

parts.note: standing with hands on hips puts the arm joints sticking outwards, which read literally gives a phrase meaning shabby

explanation.surface: A one-word puzzle about someone standing hands on hips.
explanation.walkthrough: With arms akimbo the elbows stick out; the phrase also describes a coat worn through at the sleeves, so ragged or shabby.
explanation.definitionFit: A person standing akimbo has the arm joints thrust outward, and the idiom literally describes that pose.

parts.note: reads as a lively and strange athletics race, but means smuggling liquor; 'odd' is rum and a track event is running

explanation.surface: A commentator describes a lively but peculiar race on the athletics track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' is British slang for odd, and running is a track event; the whole is smuggling alcohol, i.e. spiriting spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Smuggling illicit alcohol, as during US Prohibition, was called rum-running.

clue.text: Me first, says the terrible fellow

parts.note: the speaker's 'me' is the letter I
the van is the front or foremost part, as in vanguard

explanation.surface: A bully pushes in, insisting he comes first.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivan the Terrible was the first Tsar of Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan IV of Russia is known in history by the epithet 'the Terrible'.

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank: the missing word is the adjective Pistol uses for the pike in Henry V, Act 4, meaning mighty

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's history play with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry V the disguised King is challenged by Pistol, who asks whether he trails the mighty pike, i.e. serves as a foot soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means powerful or mighty, fitting a soldier's weapon in Pistol's bombast.

parts.note: an inspired idea, read literally as a wave sent from one mind to another as a hello

explanation.surface: Two mind-readers say hello to each other without speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: A sudden clever idea is a brainwave; a 'wave' is also a greeting gesture, so a wave sent by the mind would be a telepathic hello.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden inspiration or bright idea is a flash of thought of this kind.

clue.text: Fleet girl, but no Little Buttercup

definitions.text: Fleet girl, but no Little Buttercup

parts.words: Fleet girl, but no Little Buttercup
parts.note: the swift-footed huntress of Greek myth, whose name was also borne by ships in the Royal Navy fleet; Little Buttercup is a woman from HMS Pinafore

explanation.surface: A fast-running young woman who is not a sweet little flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' means swift and also a navy: the myth's runner shared her name with Royal Navy ships, while Little Buttercup is the bumboat woman in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera HMS Pinafore.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this huntress outran every suitor, losing only to golden apples, so she is the swift girl.

parts.note: parodies the Communist slogan 'Workers of the world, unite!', applied to detectives ('tecs') joining forces across borders

explanation.surface: A Marxist rallying cry rewritten for detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tecs' is slang for detectives; an international organisation lets police forces of many nations cooperate.
explanation.definitionFit: The International Criminal Police Organization links national police forces worldwide, a union of detectives across the globe.

clue.text: Announcement of Tommy's radio repeat performance

definitions.text: Announcement of Tommy's radio repeat performance

parts.words: Announcement of Tommy's radio repeat performance
parts.note: the catchphrase heralding comedian Tommy Handley's return each week, 'It's That Man Again', gave the radio show its initials

explanation.surface: A broadcaster announces that a comedian's show is being repeated.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Handley's wartime BBC radio comedy was called 'It's That Man Again', known by its initials; the title announces the man coming back again, a repeat appearance.
explanation.definitionFit: The show's title, abbreviated, proclaims that the same man is here once more, an announcement of his return.

explanation.surface: A paint colour chart describes a shiny shade.
explanation.definitionFit: The element is a hard silvery metal, and its compounds give a deep blue pigment used in glass and ceramics.

explanation.surface: A sports reporter praises the din coming from the terraces.
explanation.walkthrough: British football supporters once swung wooden rattles at matches; 'rattling good' is old British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent is 'rattling' in dated slang, and the clatter of fans' wooden rattles is a rattling noise.

clue.text: Sounds as if there's room for tears in Shakespeare

indicators.note: the clue says the wanted word is pronounced like the next word, so it is a soundalike

parts.note: space, the ordinary word said aloud

explanation.surface: A playgoer finds space for weeping in Shakespeare's tragedies.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare uses the word for watery discharge to mean tears, as in 'the rheum of mine eyes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Watery discharge from the eyes, Elizabethan usage for weeping, is this word in Shakespeare's plays.

explanation.surface: An odd image of the poet Byron's dark-blue undergarment.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's Childe Harold has the line 'Roll on, thou deep and dark blue Ocean, roll!'; a roll-on was an elastic girdle pulled on without fastenings.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's apostrophe to the sea begins with these two words, and an elastic girdle that is rolled onto the body bears the same name.

parts.note: a sunny ray of light is a shaft of the sun, and a broad grin goes by the same word

explanation.surface: Someone flashes a warm, cheerful grin.
explanation.walkthrough: A ray of sunshine is a sunbeam, and to grin broadly is to beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad radiant smile is called a beam, as is a ray of sunlight.

clue.text: Plenty to say at a stretch

explanation.surface: Someone talks at length when given the chance.
explanation.definitionFit: A talkative, open person is described as forthcoming in this way, and something spread out wide or extended covers a large stretch.

clue.text: Sap's rising, but not in France!

indicators.note: in a down clue the word climbs, so its letters are read from the bottom upward

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive s adding no letter

explanation.surface: In springtime the sap is rising, except, apparently, in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' in a down light turns SAP upwards to give PAS, French for 'not' as in 'ne ... pas'.
explanation.definitionFit: In French negation, ne ... pas, the second word means not.

clue.text: This way for the odour (of sanctity?)

definitions.text: This way for the odour (of sanctity?)

parts.words: This way for the odour (of sanctity?)
parts.note: reads as directions to a holy smell, but an Italian signpost pointing towards the Holy City, run together as one word, gives a pleasant smell

explanation.surface: A signpost directing visitors towards a holy fragrance.
explanation.walkthrough: Italian road signs to Rome read 'a' plus the city's Italian name; the 'odour of sanctity', a saint's fragrance, points to Rome as the seat of holiness.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasant smell or fragrance is an aroma, so it fits 'odour'.

parts.note: a wild horse of the American plains that is also the name of a famous American fighter plane, so it flies

explanation.surface: A rodeo horse bucks so hard it seems to take off.
explanation.walkthrough: The North American P-51 fighter of the Second World War shared its name with the feral horse of the American West.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild horse of the western plains carries this name, as did the P-51 fighter aircraft.

clue.text: Diplomat is security-minded — keeps artist locked up

indicators.note: the long phrase keeps the name inside it, holding letters within its words
the name is locked up within the run of words, enclosed by letters on both sides

explanation.surface: A security-conscious diplomat keeps a painter under lock and key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' and 'locked up' together say the name sits inside 'diploMAT IS SEcurity-minded'.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a French painter, a leader of Fauvism.
